sentences.text: This animal possessed a large, elongated skull and a short neck, a body shape typical of thalassophonean pliosaurids.

The holotype specimen, which serves as the primary reference for the species, is estimated to have reached a maximum length of 5.3 meters and a body mass of 2.2 tons, while other estimates suggest the genus grew to a body length of nearly 10 meters.
The genus name Brachauchenius means "short neck" in Ancient Greek and Latin, a name chosen because the original skeleton was believed to have the shortest neck of any described plesiosaur.
The only known species, Brachauchenius lucasi, was first described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1903 based on fossils found in Kansas.

The first known specimen, cataloged as USNM 4989, was collected by Charles H. Sternberg in Ottawa County, Kansas, in 1884, and the holotype skeleton was discovered nearby in the same county that year.
Additional specimens were found later, including one from Morocco that was officially assigned to the species in 2016.
A larger skull was discovered in 1950 by brothers Frank and Robert Jennrich near Fairport, Kansas, and was officially described as the new genus Megacephalosaurus eulerti in 2013.

A relatively complete pliosaurid skeleton was discovered in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, in 2000 and exhumed between 2004 and 2005, though it was initially described as Brachauchenius before being reclassified in 2016.
Photos found in 2007 revealed that the Fairport skull had underside features distinct from other Brachauchenius lucasi skulls.

Microscopic analysis in 2005 dated the holotype, which was discovered in 1884 near Delphos, Ottawa County, Kansas, to the early Middle Turonian based on its origin in the Greenhorn Limestone or Fairport Chalk.
Brachauchenius lived during the Late Cretaceous in regions that are now North America and North Africa.

It is debated whether some specimens currently attributed to Brachauchenius actually belong to the genus Megacephalosaurus. Later analyses showed that a Colombian specimen referred to Brachauchenius was distinct enough to warrant a new genus and species, named Stenorhynchosaurus munozi. The specimen FHSM VP-321 was later assigned to its own genus and species, Megacephalosaurus eulerti.
The skeleton of Stenorhynchosaurus munozi dates to the Upper Barremian, representing the oldest known example of the brachauchenines.
